approaches.name: Pediatric lateral or medial parapatellar arthrotomy
approaches.region: pediatric anterior knee and distal femur
approaches.corridor: Limited parapatellar capsular incision adjacent to the patellar tendon, selected on the fracture side

procedure_applications.condition: A pediatric epiphyseal or articular fracture requires direct visualization through a limited medial or lateral parapatellar window

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with the knee freely flexed and the injured side of the joint accessible.

setup.text: Review CT or MRI when needed to define the epiphyseal fracture, choose the side that best exposes the target, and prepare fluoroscopy and physeal-respecting fixation.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark patella, patellar-tendon borders, joint line, tibial tubercle, and involved femoral condyle.

incision.text: Begin beside the patellar tendon at midpatellar level and extend initially to the joint line; lengthen only as required for articular reduction.

superficial_interval.text: Develop a limited parapatellar tract without broad skin flaps or unnecessary extensor-mechanism stripping.

deep_interval.text: Incise capsule in the skin-incision plane and use gentle retractors for direct fracture visualization; keep sharp dissection away from the meniscus.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, parapatellar retinacular-capsular layer, synovium, then articular fracture.

structures_encountered.text: Patellar tendon, retinaculum, capsule, synovium, meniscus, femoral condyle, physis, and epiphyseal fragment may be encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Meniscus, articular cartilage, patellar tendon, infrapatellar saphenous branches medially, and the distal-femoral physis are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Avoid sharp dissection around the meniscus and repeated manipulation across the injured physis.

retraction_hazards.text: Use small blunt retractors under direct vision and avoid levering on pediatric cartilage or the patellar tendon.

exposure.text: Provides targeted direct visualization of the selected femoral condyle and articular surface with limited soft-tissue disruption.

limitations.text: The limited window is inadequate for complex bicondylar or posterior fractures that cannot be reduced under direct vision.

extensions.text: Lengthen proximally or distally along the chosen parapatellar side when additional articular visualization is necessary.

indications.text: Use for selected pediatric articular and epiphyseal fractures needing limited direct reduction and fixation.

relative_contraindications.text: Choose a broader lateral, medial, or extensile parapatellar exposure when the fracture cannot be visualized and controlled through a limited arthrotomy.

implant_implications.text: Place implants under direct and fluoroscopic control to restore the joint while minimizing avoidable physeal and cartilage violation.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use orthogonal and tangential views to verify articular congruity, physeal alignment, trajectory, and implant containment.

closure.text: Repair the capsule with absorbable suture after hemostasis, then close subcutaneous tissue and skin routinely.

complications.text: Complications include meniscal or chondral injury, growth arrest, stiffness, infection, malreduction, and fixation failure.

bailouts.text: Extend or convert the exposure when fracture visualization remains inadequate rather than performing blind reduction or fixation.

questions.question: Where does the initial incision run?
questions.answer: Adjacent to the patellar tendon from midpatella to the joint line.

questions.question: What structure must sharp dissection avoid?
When is the incision extended?
questions.answer: When more articular exposure is needed for reduction and fixation.

approaches.name: Pediatric medial approach to the distal femur
approaches.corridor: Posterior border of vastus medialis with optional proximal extension between vastus medialis and adductor magnus

procedure_applications.condition: A medial Salter-Harris II, medial articular or Hoffa fracture needs direct reduction, or vascular injury requires medial access

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with the knee flexed to relax medial tissues and permit posterior sartorial retraction.

setup.text: Identify the tension-side reduction block on imaging, map the physis and vascular status, and have vascular support available when arterial injury is suspected.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark medial joint line, adductor tubercle, posterior vastus-medialis border, patella, physis, and metaphyseal fragment.

incision.text: Use a 4-5 cm straight incision from the joint line proximally along the posterior vastus-medialis border, extending as needed.

superficial_interval.text: Identify, incise, and mobilize the distal posterior edge of vastus medialis while protecting medial sensory and venous structures.

deep_interval.text: Retract vastus medialis anteriorly to expose physis and metaphysis; for proximal/posterior extension retract sartorius and adductor magnus posteriorly while remaining on bone.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, vastus-medialis fascia, medial muscle interval, periosteum and physis, with optional posterior adductor plane.

structures_encountered.text: Vastus medialis, entrapped periosteum, physis, distal metaphysis, sartorius, adductor-magnus tendon, capsule, and popliteal space may be encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Popliteal artery and vein, tibial nerve, saphenous structures, medial genicular vessels, physis, periosteal blood supply, and cartilage are at risk.

danger_zones.text: The popliteal bundle lies immediately posterior to the femur; all posterior extension must be blunt, controlled, and kept on bone.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid forceful posterior retraction, epiphyseal stripping, or repeated reduction across the high-risk distal-femoral physis.

exposure.text: Exposes medial physis and metaphysis directly, with extensions for medial articular lesions, limited posterior access, or vascular exploration.

limitations.text: Posterior articular visualization remains limited and broad anterior articular reconstruction may require a parapatellar approach.

extensions.text: Extend proximally to sartorius and adductor magnus, bluntly develop posterior access, or add a capsulotomy for selected joint inspection.

indications.text: Use after failed closed reduction of medial Salter-Harris II fractures and for medial Hoffa, osteochondral, tumor, or vascular-associated lesions.

relative_contraindications.text: Choose another approach when broad anterior or direct posterior visualization is required or medial soft tissue is compromised.

implant_implications.text: Remove entrapped periosteum, restore physeal anatomy, and use stable fixation with minimal additional physeal or posterior neurovascular risk.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm physeal and articular alignment, medial implant position, and guarded screw length on orthogonal and oblique views.

closure.text: Repair capsulotomy or fascia as used, allow vastus medialis to return anatomically, obtain hemostasis, and close in layers.

complications.text: Complications include popliteal or saphenous injury, growth arrest, deformity, limb-length discrepancy, stiffness, infection, and malreduction.

bailouts.text: Stop blind posterior dissection and add a dedicated exposure or vascular assistance when safe control cannot be achieved.

questions.question: What commonly blocks Salter-Harris II reduction?
questions.answer: Entrapped periosteum attached to the distal epiphyseal fragment.

approaches.name: Pediatric safe corridors for distal-femur spanning external fixation
aliases: pediatric femur tibia pin safe zones
approaches.corridor: Anterolateral or direct-lateral femoral and anteromedial tibial percutaneous pin corridors

procedure_applications.condition: Temporary knee-spanning stabilization is required with protection of physes, neurovascular structures, and definitive surgical corridors

positioning.text: Position supine with the full limb accessible and imageable from femur through tibia.

setup.text: Map both physes, soft-tissue injury, neurovascular anatomy, and future fixation paths before placing any pin.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark femoral shaft, distal-femoral physis, vastus lateralis, iliotibial band, fibular head, tibial crest, and planned definitive incisions.

incision.text: Use adequate small incisions and blunt dissection to bone to prevent skin and muscle tethering.

superficial_interval.text: Approach femur between rectus and vastus lateralis or directly lateral while avoiding iliotibial tract; approach tibia about 1 cm medial to the crest.

deep_interval.text: Use sleeves to bone, obtain controlled bicortical purchase without medial femoral plunge, and angle tibial pins approximately 20 degrees from sagittal away from posterolateral structures.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, anterior-lateral thigh muscle to femur; skin and subcutaneous tissue directly to anteromedial tibia.

structures_encountered.text: Rectus-vastus interval, vastus lateralis, femoral periosteum, tibial crest, and anteromedial tibial cortex are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Distal-femoral physis, medial femoral vessels, sciatic nerve, common and deep peroneal nerves, anterior tibial vessels, saphenous nerve, and definitive operative planes are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Keep distal femoral pins at least 2 cm proximal to the physis; avoid medial overpenetration, fibular-head pinning, and posterolateral tibial trajectories.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid iliotibial-band tethering, thermal necrosis, drill plunge, and tight skin around pins.

exposure.text: Provides pediatric-safe skeletal purchase for temporary stabilization while preserving growth plates and definitive fixation corridors.

limitations.text: Published safe zones remain guides; patient size, fracture displacement, soft-tissue injury, and physeal location require individual imaging.

extensions.text: Add or relocate pins only after remapping physes and neurovascular and definitive-treatment corridors.

indications.text: Use for staged damage-control stabilization of unstable pediatric distal-femur injuries when definitive treatment must be delayed.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid injured or infected skin and any corridor where the physis or neurovascular anatomy cannot be reliably localized.

implant_implications.text: Keep pins outside the future nail, plate, and incision paths and preserve sufficient distance from fracture and physis.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm physeal clearance, bicortical purchase without overpenetration, joint clearance, and frame alignment on orthogonal views.

closure.text: Release tethered skin, dress pin sites, and document distal perfusion and nerve function after frame construction.

complications.text: Complications include physeal injury, neurovascular injury, pin-track infection, thermal injury, fracture propagation, stiffness, and contamination of definitive corridors.

bailouts.text: If physis or safe trajectory is uncertain, stop and relocate under imaging or direct exposure rather than accepting a hazardous pin.

questions.question: How far from the distal-femoral physis should a pin be?
What are the safest femoral regions?
Why avoid the iliotibial tract?
questions.answer: To reduce loosening and pin-track infection from tethered motion.
